title: Built our roguelite deckbuilder with 100% ai code and assets - looking for feedback
author: beelllllll
selftext:
Me and a few friends built **For The Realm**, a multiplayer first roguelite deckbuilder, in about 3 months.

The code was **100% AI created** using **Claude Code** and **Codex** on the $100/month plans. We also used **AutoSprite** for all the Assets including characters, particle effects, environment props all that.

We’re in the final stretch now doing playtesting, polish, and Steam page cleanup.

Would love honest feedback:

* Does the game look fun?
* Does the trailer make the core gameplay clear?
* What’s the weakest-looking part: art, UI, trailer, gameplay, or messaging?

Steam: [**https://store.steampowered.com/app/3040260/For\_The\_Realm/**](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3040260/For_The_Realm/)

Happy to answer anything about the workflow too.

comments.author: ffxivthrowaway03
comments.body:
I'm gonna be honest leaning towards curt, I stopped reading at "roguelite deckbuilder," and most other people are too.

You didn't make Slay The Spire.  You're not gonna make Slay The Spire.  Someone else already made Slay The Spire. This market segment is *extremely* saturated already and is getting worse every single day.  By the time you finish this game you're gonna see another 500 posts of people's vibe coded STS ripoffs with basic AI art assets come and go.

If this was a passion project built with years of effort and love, had an *obsessive* level of design refinement, and looked *much, much, much* better than it does?  Maybe you've got a chance to compete in the "roguelite deckbuilder" space.  But the 15 second glance is "this is another cheap AI Slay The Spire ripoff.  Nobody wants that, nobody's buying that, nobody's playing that.

If you really want to make a game in this space and it's not just a cheap pump and dump clone, my advice to you is spend a whole lot more effort differentiating yourself from STS, not copying it almost verbatim.

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
I'd honestly advise against that too, and here's why.

Have you played the Slay the Spire board game?  If not, you should play it with your friends as dev research.  It *pointedly* illustrates the problem with multiplayer in a roguelite deckbuilder - **there is one objective, right answer to every play*****.***  Quick summary- in the STS board game it's fully cooperative, and everyone can play their cards in whatever order they see fit.  But it's... still STS.  Which means everyone's symmetrical, simultaneous play devolves into "All four player's cards are really just one singular mega-hand" and it falls right back into the STS design of each card *absolutely should* be played in a specific order.

That's not fun cooperative board game, that's *leaning into* the bugbear that designers in the co-op board game space have been desperately trying to design themselves away from - one person at the table becomes the Master Of What To Do and just tells everyone else exactly how they should play their cards for optimal play.  Every.  Turn.  At which point the other players simply shouldn't even be at the table anymore, and if they *choose* to do something else it's technically a misplay and Master Of What To Do starts getting snippy.  It's a recipe for friction between players, it's objectively poor design that I'm honestly surprised the STS board game designers so wantonly fell into. It's bad, and feels bad.  It feels like playing Magic The Gathering by committee, nobody wants that.

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
If you're going to do AI art assets and want consistency, you'll *never* get it from a multimodal generative model like Claude/ChatGPT/Gemini.  It simply cannot do it no matter how hard you prompt and tell it to reference things.

You'll need to build a stable diffusion based pipeline (or pay through the nose for some fly by night wrapper for someone elses).  Use the multimodal models or hand sketches for rough outlines then push them through img2img/IPadapter/controlnet driven workflows to use the original generation as a composition guideline while using your new prompt/model/LoRAs to apply *style* to the structure. Then manually take the results into Photoshop and clean them up, make sure color palette/tone/etc are consistent, etc.  It won't be perfect, but it'll get a hell of a lot closer than yoloing prompts and crossing your fingers.

comments.author: Alternative-Bread411
comments.body:
Brutally honest TLDR: The highly detail cutscenes look like derivative slop, AI is letting you down here. The in-game visuals are intriguing and remind me of PSX era FF games. The creative direction in an issue. I'm not getting a sense of a cohesive world that makes me want to learn more. The characters feel like they're pulled from entirely different games, so there's a lack of identity tying everything together.

The environment art also feels very first pass at the moment. Music is repetitive.

From a gameplay perspective, deck-building roguelikes are a heavily saturated genre, so having a strong visual identity and world is going to be especially important for standing out. AI is great at asset generation, not at creating the exceptional, you'll need the latter to compete.

If AI were an ingredient then too much would make a product bland. Worth considering.
